  • When crossing two fertile independent transgenic lines (A and B), the failure to recover double-transgenic progeny indicates that the interaction between the protein products of genes A and B is lethal to the developing zygote or embryo.
✅ Correct Answer: Interaction between products of genes A and B is lethal to the zygote.

question: The range of transformation frequencies obtained in independent transformation experiments using four different constructs with different combinations of promoters (Pr) and selection marker genes, is given below: Construct Transformation frequency CaMV35S Pr – bar – nos polyA 20% – 35% Nos Pr – bar – nos polyA 2% – 4% CaMV35S Pr – NPTII – nos polyA 46% – 49% Nos Pr – NPTII – nos polyA 24% – 28% In the absence of any other factors, which one of the following statements is NOT acceptable as a logical conclusion based on the above data?
options: Use of stronger promoters for expression of selection marker genes can increase transformation frequencies.
Variations in expression levels between the NPTII and bar genes is not influenced by the nos poly A signal.
Production of herbicide resistant plants at high frequency can be achieved with lower expression levels of the transgene.
Use of kanamycin as a selection marker appears to be more favorable for production of larger number of transgenic plants.
correct_answer: Production of herbicide resistant plants at high frequency can be achieved with lower expression levels of the transgene.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Selectable Marker Expression Levels:
  • Herbicide resistance genes (such as bar or CP4-EPSPS) provide robust selection because only moderate enzymatic expression is sufficient to detoxify the herbicide and allow shoot regeneration at high frequency.
✅ Correct Answer: Production of herbicide resistant plants at high frequency can be achieved with lower expression levels of the transgene.

question: Callus-mediated regeneration is NOT preferred for micropropagation because:
options: it takes longer time for regeneration.
plant regeneration is problematic due to poor organogenesis
it leads to generation of variants
hardening of plants is difficult to achieve.
correct_answer: it leads to generation of variants
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Somaclonal Variation in Micropropagation:
  • In commercial micropropagation, true-to-type clonal fidelity is critical.
  • Plant regeneration through an intermediate undifferentiated callus phase induces high rates of somaclonal variation (chromosomal rearrangements, point mutations, epigenetic changes), leading to undesirable phenotypic variants. Direct organogenesis or axillary branching is therefore preferred.
✅ Correct Answer: it leads to generation of variants

question: In a transgenic plant, the phenomenon of Co-suppression is due to:
options: transgene integration within the endogenous gene
transgene integration at a locus very close to the endogenous gene
similarity between the transgene and endogenous gene sequences
lack of similarity between the transgene and endogenous gene sequences
correct_answer: similarity between the transgene and endogenous gene sequences
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Co-Suppression (RNA Interference) in Transgenic Plants:
  • First discovered in petunias (Napoli and Jorgensen) when introducing an extra transgenic copy of chalcone synthase:
  • Instead of deeper purple flowers, white or variegated flowers were produced because both the transgene and the homologous endogenous gene were simultaneously silenced.
  • This co-suppression is triggered by high sequence similarity between the transgene and the endogenous gene, which triggers double-stranded RNA formation and Dicer-mediated PTGS.
✅ Correct Answer: similarity between the transgene and endogenous gene sequences

question: In inbred lines, gene and genotypic frequencies are maintained by growing them in isolation followed by:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Maintaining Inbred Line Genotypic Frequencies:
  • In plant breeding, inbred lines are maintained at genetic equilibrium through controlled random mating (or selfing) in isolation without directional selection.
✅ Correct Answer: random mating without selection

question: Homozygous plants from bi-parental mating for development of mapping populations can be obtained in a short time by:
options: random mating in F2 followed by selfing in subsequent generations
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Rapid Homozygosity via Doubled Haploids:
  • Traditional inbreeding requires 6-8 generations of selfing to achieve $>99\%$ homozygosity.
  • The Doubled Haploid (DH) technique cultures haploid microspores/pollen from $F_1$ plants and doubles their chromosome number using colchicine. This achieves 100% complete homozygosity at all loci in a single generation, greatly accelerating mapping population development.
✅ Correct Answer: development of doubled haploids

question: Which one of the following is NOT required for QTL analysis in association mapping?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Association Mapping (GWAS) vs Linkage Mapping:
  • Linkage mapping: Requires bi-parental mapping populations ($F_2$, RILs, DH) and a pre-constructed genetic linkage map.
  • Association mapping (GWAS): Exploits historical recombination in diverse natural populations or germplasm collections; it evaluates statistical associations between genotypes and phenotypes without requiring a formal pedigree-based genetic linkage map.
✅ Correct Answer: Genetic linkage map

question: Which one of the following hormones promote production of seedless grapes?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Parthenocarpy Induced by Gibberellins ($GA_3$):
  • Application of Gibberellic acid ($GA_3$) to flowers stimulates ovary growth and pericarp development in the absence of pollination and fertilization (parthenocarpy), commercially producing large, high-quality seedless grapes and fruits.
✅ Correct Answer: GA3

question: Which one of the following molecular markers is associated with bacterial blight resistance in rice?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bacterial Blight Resistance in Rice (Xa21 Gene):
  • Xa21 is a well-characterized receptor kinase gene cloned from wild rice (Oryza longistaminata).
  • It confers broad-spectrum resistance to bacterial blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae) and is widely used as a molecular marker in marker-assisted selection programs.
✅ Correct Answer: Xa21

question: Match the proteins in Group I with members in Group II Group I Group II 1 Alkaline phosphatase P Extracellular 2 Fo component of ATP synthase Q Cytoplasm 3 Alcohol dehydrogenase R Inner membrane 4 Pectinase S Periplasm
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Plant Defense Proteins & Classification:
  • Matching plant defense and structural proteins across functional categories gives 1-S; 2-R; 3-Q; 4-P.
✅ Correct Answer: 1-S; 2-R; 3-Q; 4-P

question: Application of the herbicide, phosphoinothricin, results in death of plants due to accumulation of:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mechanism of Phosphinothricin (Glufosinate) Action:
  • Phosphinothricin (PPT) is a structural analog of glutamate that potently inhibits Glutamine synthetase (GS).
  • Inhibition of GS prevents the assimilation of ammonium ($ ext{NH}_4^+$) into glutamine.
  • This causes a catastrophic, toxic accumulation of ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) in plant tissues, which uncouples photophosphorylation, destroys chloroplasts, and causes rapid plant death.
✅ Correct Answer: NH3

question: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of Agrobacterium VirE protein?
options: Its synthesis is induced by VirG protein
It contains a nuclear localization signal
It protects T-DNA from being destroyed by plant defense mechanism
It is a component of T-pilus
correct_answer: It is a component of T-pilus
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Agrobacterium VirE2 Single-Stranded Binding Protein:
  • VirE2 is a single-stranded DNA-binding protein (SSB) that coats the single-stranded T-DNA strand, protecting it from plant nucleases and helping form a compact telephone cord-like structure.
  • VirB proteins (VirB1-VirB11) and VirD4 form the Type IV secretion system and T-pilus. VirE2 is NOT a structural component of the T-pilus.
✅ Correct Answer: It is a component of T-pilus

question: Transgenic potato plants with high amylose starch were developed by:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Starch Biosynthesis Engineering (High Amylose Potato):
  • Starch consists of linear amylose and branched amylopectin.
  • Starch branching enzymes (SBE I and SBE II) introduce $alpha-(1 ightarrow 6)$ glycosidic branch points to form amylopectin.
  • Suppression / antisense silencing of starch branching enzymes eliminates branching, shifting virtually all glucose polymerization into linear chains and yielding potatoes with exceptionally high amylose content ($>70\%$).
✅ Correct Answer: suppression of starch branching enzymes

question: Developing cisgenic disease resistant apple is advantageous over conventional breeding because:
options: genes cannot be transferred from sexually compatible species through pollination due to hybridization barriers.
apple is vegetatively propagated and produces sterile seeds.
cisgenes will not disrupt endogenous genes when introduced by Agrobacterium mediated transformation.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Advantages of Cisgenics over Conventional Breeding:
  • Cisgenics: The genetic modification of a recipient plant with a natural gene (including its native promoter and terminator) isolated from the same species or a sexually compatible relative.
  • Unlike conventional introgression backcrossing, which introduces large chunks of donor chromosome containing deleterious linked genes (linkage drag), cisgenics transfers strictly the gene of interest with zero linkage drag.
✅ Correct Answer: there is no linkage drag.

question: For development of selection marker-free transgenic plants by co-transformation using Agrobacterium, the marker genes are:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Marker-Free Transgenic Plants by Co-Transformation:
  • In co-transformation, the gene of interest (GOI) and the selectable marker gene are placed on separate plasmids (or separate T-DNAs).
  • If the two T-DNAs integrate at different, unlinked chromosomal loci, selfing the $T_0$ plant produces $T_1$ progeny where the marker gene segregates away (segregates out in the $T_1$ generation), leaving marker-free transgenic plants.
✅ Correct Answer: segregated out in T1 generation

question: Breakdown of Bt- mediated insect resistance in crops can be delayed by:
options: Cultivation of different Bt cotton varieties with same Bt gene
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Refugia Strategy for Insect Resistance Management:
  • Planting a non-Bt refuge plot alongside transgenic Bt crops ensures the survival of homozygous susceptible ($ss$) insect pests, diluting rare recessive resistance alleles ($rr$) and effectively delaying the breakdown of Bt-mediated resistance.
✅ Correct Answer: Refugia strategy

question: Which one of the following is matched INCORRECTLY?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Herbicide Resistance Genes (bar gene):
  • The bar gene (isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus) encodes phosphinothricin acetyltransferase (PAT), which acetylates and detoxifies the herbicide glufosinate / phosphinothricin.
  • It confers resistance to herbicides, NOT resistance to viruses.
✅ Correct Answer: bar gene – resistance to viruses

question: Which one of the following would produce androgenic haploids in anther culture?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Androgenic Haploid Production via Anther Culture:
  • In anther/pollen culture, androgenic haploids are produced through embryogenesis originating from uninucleate young microspores (pollen grains at the uninucleate to early binucleate developmental stage).
✅ Correct Answer: Young microspores

question: Male sterility in plants is induced by expression of the TA29-barnase-pA cassette in:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Engineered Genetic Male Sterility (Barnase-Barstar System):
  • In the Mariani male sterility system (used in hybrid mustard, Brassica napus):
  • The cytotoxic ribonuclease gene barnase is driven by the TA29 promoter, which is active strictly in the tapetum layer of the developing anther.
  • Destruction of the tapetum deprives developing pollen of nutrients, resulting in complete male sterility without affecting female fertility.
✅ Correct Answer: Tapetum

question: Anchorage dependent CHO cells are grown by aeration using micro carrier beads. The maximum detrimental effect of shear occurs due to agitation if the size (Kolmogorov scale) of eddies is:
options: lesser than the size of the beads
equal to the size of beads
larger than the size of beads
independent of the size of beads
correct_answer: lesser than the size of the beads
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Microcarrier Culture for Anchorage-Dependent Cells:
  • In microcarrier suspension cultures (e.g. Cytodex beads), the Kolmogorov eddy length scale ($eta$) determines hydrodynamic shear damage: $$eta = \left(\frac{\nu^3}{\epsilon}\right)^{1/4}$$
  • Cell damage occurs when the turbulent eddy size is comparable to or smaller than the size of the microcarrier beads, because the beads become trapped and buffeted within turbulent eddies.
✅ Correct Answer: lesser than the size of the beads

question: With progress in the growth of E. coli in a minimal medium (constant aeration and agitation), the dissolved oxygen (DO) initially declined and then started to increase. If the DO again starts to decrease on addition of glucose, then the most probable explanation is:
options: decrease in solubility of oxygen occurred due to glucose addition
decrease in the number of cells takes place due to cell lysis
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Monod Growth Kinetics & Substrate Limitation:
  • In minimal media containing glucose and inorganic salts, as bacterial biomass accumulates, the specific growth rate eventually decelerates because growth becomes limited by glucose depletion.
✅ Correct Answer: growth is limited by glucose

question: An organism obeys Andrews model for growth inhibition with Ks and Ki values of 0.01 g/l and 1.0 g/l respectively. If the substrate is present at an initial concentration of 1.0g/l, the specific growth rate of the culture upon entering log phase would be approximately:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Andrews Model for Substrate Inhibition:
  • Andrews kinetics equation: $$\mu = \frac{\mu_{\max} S}{K_s + S + \frac{S^2}{K_i}}$$
  • Substituting given parameters at specified concentrations yields 1/2 of μmax.
✅ Correct Answer: 1/2 of μmax

question: In a stirred tank reactor when the agitation rate is increased, the kL and kLa values will:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Impeller Agitation and Mass Transfer Parameters ($K_L$ and $a$):
  • Increasing agitation speed ($N$) in a stirred tank bioreactor:
    1. Increases turbulent shear, breaking bubbles into smaller sizes $\implies$ dramatically increases specific interfacial surface area ($a$).
    2. Thins the liquid boundary film surrounding gas bubbles $\implies$ increases liquid mass transfer coefficient ($K_L$).
  • Therefore, both $K_L$ and $a$ increase.
✅ Correct Answer: both increase

question: Which one of the following is correct regarding cell damage in an agitated and sparged mammalian cell bioreactor?
options: High shear stress arising during mixing of the cell culture is the major cause of cell damage.
Shear stress arising from the breakup of bubbles at the liquid surface is a major cause of cell damage.
Shear stress between bubbles in the foam at the liquid surface is a major cause of cell damage
Using agitator blades of a radial flow type with mirror finish reduces shear and hence cell damage
correct_answer: Shear stress arising from the breakup of bubbles at the liquid surface is a major cause of cell damage.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sparging-Induced Shear Damage in Animal Cell Cultures:
  • Mammalian cells lack a rigid cell wall and are sensitive to shear.
  • Extensive studies (e.g. Papoutsakis) demonstrated that cell death in sparged bioreactors occurs primarily in the foam layer at the surface, where rapid bubble burst and liquid film retraction generate intense localized hydrodynamic stresses.
✅ Correct Answer: Shear stress arising from the breakup of bubbles at the liquid surface is a major cause of cell damage.

question: Which one of the statements given below is NOT true? Equilibrium constant (K) of a chemical reaction at a specific temperature can be determined if the:
options: ΔG0 of the reaction is known
Equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products are known
ΔH and ΔS of the reaction are known
ΔH and initial concentrations of the reactants and products are known
correct_answer: ΔH and initial concentrations of the reactants and products are known
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemical Equilibrium Constants and Thermodynamics:
  • Equilibrium constant $K_{\text{eq}}$ is related to standard Gibbs free energy: $$\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K_{\text{eq}}$$
  • Enthalpy ($Delta H$) alone is insufficient to calculate $K_{\text{eq}}$ without entropy ($Delta S$), and equilibrium concentrations do not depend on initial concentrations. Thus, the statement claiming $K_{\text{eq}}$ can be determined from $Delta H$ and initial concentrations alone is NOT true.
✅ Correct Answer: ΔH and initial concentrations of the reactants and products are known

question: If a big centrifuge with the bowl diameter of 1m rotates at 60 rpm, at what speed (rpm) does a smaller centrifuge with a diameter of 0.5 m need to be operated for achieving the same separation factor?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Centrifuge Separation Factor ($G$-force Scaling):
  • Separation factor (relative centrifugal force, RCF): $$\text{RCF} \propto r \cdot \omega^2 \propto D \cdot N^2$$ where $D$ is bowl diameter and $N$ is rotation speed in rpm.
  • For equal separation factor ($D_1 N_1^2 = D_2 N_2^2$): $$N_2 = N_1 \sqrt{\frac{D_1}{D_2}}$$
  • Given: $D_1 = 1\text{ m}$, $N_1 = 60\text{ rpm}$, $D_2 = 0.5\text{ m}$: $$N_2 = 60 \sqrt{\frac{1.0}{0.5}} = 60 \sqrt{2} = 60 \times 1.414 \approx 84.85\text{ rpm} \approx 85\text{ rpm}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 85

question: What is the linear flow rate (superficial velocity in cm/h) in a chromatographic column of 1.0 cm inner diameter with a bed porosity of 0.8 when the volumetric flow rate is 1 ml/min?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Superficial Linear Velocity in Chromatography:
  • Column inner diameter $D = 1.0\text{ cm} \implies$ radius $r = 0.5\text{ cm}$.
  • Cross-sectional area: $$A = \pi r^2 = 3.1416 \times (0.5)^2 = 0.7854\text{ cm}^2$$
  • Volumetric flow rate $Q = 1\text{ mL/min} = 60\text{ mL/h} = 60\text{ cm}^3\text{/h}$.
  • Superficial velocity ($u_s$): $$u_s = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{60\text{ cm}^3\text{/h}}{0.7854\text{ cm}^2} \approx 76.39\text{ cm/h} \approx 76.4\text{ cm/h}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 76.4

question: For a cell growth process, the units for yield, productivity and titre are:
options: gg-1, gl-1h-1 and g g-1l-1 h-1
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Fermentation Performance Metrics & Units:
  • Biomass Yield ($Y_{X/S}$): Grams of biomass produced per gram of substrate consumed $\implies \mathbf{g \cdot g^{-1}}$.
  • Productivity ($Q_P$): Grams of product formed per liter of reactor volume per hour $\implies \mathbf{g \cdot L^{-1} \cdot h^{-1}}$.
  • Titre: Final concentration of product in the broth $\implies \mathbf{g \cdot L^{-1}}$.
✅ Correct Answer: gg-1, gl-1h-1 and gl-1

question: In a fermentor the impeller diameter is increased from 0.5 m to 1 m and the rpm is increased from 100 rpm to 400 rpm. Reynolds number will increase by?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Power Consumption in Aerated / Non-Aerated Fermenters:
  • Power number in turbulent regime: $$P = N_p \rho N^3 D_i^5$$
  • Doubling the impeller diameter ($D_i$ from $0.5\text{ m}$ to $1.0\text{ m}$) under constant tip speed condition or scaled parameters increases power input by 16-fold ($2^4 = 16$).
✅ Correct Answer: 16 fold

question: Zymomonas mobilis is cultivated in a 60 l chemostat. The μmax and Ks values are 0.2 h- 1 and 0.5 g l-1 respectively. The flow rate (l h-1) required for a steady state substrate concentration of 0.5 g l-1 in the reactor is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemostat Operating Dynamics & Dilution Rate:
  • For Zymomonas mobilis in a 60 L chemostat with specified kinetic parameters ($mu_{\max}$, $K_s$), calculating the steady-state substrate consumption and effluent volumetric throughput yields 6.
✅ Correct Answer: 6

question: Which one of the following statements is WRONG for conventional batch filtration of a mycelial fermentation broth?
options: Blockage of the membrane pores by cell debris
The specific cake resistance remains constant
compressible cake deposition on the membrane
correct_answer: The specific cake resistance remains constant
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cake Filtration Theory & Specific Cake Resistance:
  • In conventional dead-end cake filtration: $$\frac{t}{V} = \frac{\mu \alpha c}{2 A^2 \Delta P} V + \frac{\mu R_m}{A \Delta P}$$
  • For incompressible cakes, the specific cake resistance ($\alpha$) is constant. However, biological biomass cakes (mycelia, bacterial cells) are highly compressible.
  • As filtration pressure increases and cake depth grows, compressive stresses compact the cellular structure, causing the specific cake resistance ($\alpha$) to increase substantially over time. Thus, claiming specific cake resistance remains constant is WRONG.
✅ Correct Answer: The specific cake resistance remains constant

question: The reason for the choice of E. coli for the production of ethanol from lignocellulose is because it:
options: grows efficiently in various hexoses and pentoses
can be grown to high cell density
can tolerate very high concentration of ethanol
correct_answer: grows efficiently in various hexoses and pentoses
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Engineered E. coli for Bioethanol Production:
  • Lignocellulosic biomass hydrolysates contain a mixture of both 6-carbon hexose sugars (glucose, mannose, galactose) and 5-carbon pentose sugars (xylose, arabinose).
  • Saccharomyces cerevisiae cannot naturally ferment pentose sugars. In contrast, Escherichia coli naturally utilizes and metabolizes all common hexose and pentose sugars via the Embden-Meyerhof and pentose phosphate pathways. Engineered ethanologenic E. coli (carrying Zymomonas mobilis pdc and adh genes) efficiently ferments all biomass sugars to ethanol.
✅ Correct Answer: grows efficiently in various hexoses and pentoses

question: Two organisms A and B with the same μmax and Yx/s are cultivated independently in batch culture. They have Ks values of 1 g.l-1 and 3 g.l-1 respectively. Given that the initial substrate concentration was 5 g/l, which of the following is TRUE after complete exhaustion of the substrate?
options: Organism A will have lower average specific growth rate than B.
Organism A will have higher average specific growth rate than B.
Both the organisms would have same average specific growth rate.
The final biomass achieved in B would be higher than in A.
correct_answer: Organism A will have higher average specific growth rate than B.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Growth Kinetics in Transient Bioreactors:
  • Comparing growth rates under fluctuating substrate conditions: Organism A, with lower affinity threshold, achieves a higher average specific growth rate than B.
✅ Correct Answer: Organism A will have higher average specific growth rate than B.

question: Pseudomonas with the elemental composition of CH3O0.5N0.5 (MW = 30) is grown in a bioreactor to a final cell mass of 30 g/l. The minimum concentration (g/l) of ammonia (NH3) (MW = 17) (as the sole nitrogen source) required is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Degree of Reductance & Theoretical Yield:
  • For Pseudomonas with elemental composition $\text{CH}_3\text{O}_{0.5}\text{N}_{0.5}$ (MW = 31):
  • Degree of reductance ($\gamma$): $$\gamma = 4(1) + 1(3) - 2(0.5) - 3(0.5) = 4 + 3 - 1 - 1.5 = 4.5$$
  • Performing electron mass balance and stoichiometry yields 8.5.
✅ Correct Answer: 8.5

question: To reduce the level of deactivation of media components for culturing Lactobacillus spp., a high temperature and short time (HTST) regime is used for sterilization, PRIMARILY because:
options: Deactivation energy of contaminants > Deactivation energy of medium components
Deactivation energy of contaminants < Deactivation energy of medium components
Deactivation energy of contaminants = Deactivation energy of medium components
the time required for sterilization is reduced
correct_answer: Deactivation energy of contaminants > Deactivation energy of medium components
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Thermal Inactivation Kinetics (HTST Sterilization):
  • The thermal destruction of heat-resistant bacterial endospores (e.g. Geobacillus stearothermophilus) has a very high activation energy ($E_{a,\text{spores}} \approx 280 - 350\text{ kJ/mol}$).
  • In contrast, the thermal degradation/deactivation of nutrient media components (vitamins, amino acids, sugars) has a much lower activation energy ($E_{a,\text{nutrients}} \approx 80 - 120\text{ kJ/mol}$).
  • Because $E_{a,\text{contaminants}} > E_{a,\text{medium components}}$, High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) sterilization kills spores exponentially faster while preserving delicate nutrients.
✅ Correct Answer: Deactivation energy of contaminants > Deactivation energy of medium components

question: Acetobacter aceti converts alcohol to acetic acid according to the stoichiometric relation C2H5OH + O2 CH3COOH + H2O In a vigorously agitated and aerated reactor containing 20 g/l ethanol, the organism produces 16 g/l acetic acid and 2 g/l was the residual ethanol concentration. What are the theoretical and observed yields of acetic acid expressed in g/g ethanol?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Stoichiometry of Acetic Acid Fermentation:
  • Reaction: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
  • Molecular weights:
    • $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} = 46\text{ g/mol}$
    • $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} = 60\text{ g/mol}$
    • $\text{O}_2 = 32\text{ g/mol}$
    • $\text{H}_2\text{O} = 18\text{ g/mol}$
  • Yield of acetic acid per g alcohol = $\frac{60}{46}$.
  • Stoichiometric ratio of oxygen to water = $\frac{16}{18}$.
✅ Correct Answer: 60/46 and 16/18

question: A continuous stirred tank bioreactor produces 48 kg lysine.day-1. If the volumetric productivity is 2 g.l-1.h-1, the volume of the reactor is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bioreactor Volume for Lysine Production:
  • Target production = $48\text{ kg/day} = 2.0\text{ kg/h} = 2000\text{ g/h}$.
  • Using volumetric productivity rate ($2\text{ g/(L}\cdot\text{h)}$): $$V = \frac{2000\text{ g/h}}{2\text{ g/(L}\cdot\text{h)}} = 1000\text{ L} = 1.0\text{ m}^3$$
✅ Correct Answer: 1 m3

question: Aqueous Two Phase System (ATPS) is used to isolate a protease from a fermentation broth. The partition coefficient (K) is 2.5. For 80 % recovery of protease in a single step, the volume ratios of upper and the lower phases should be:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Aqueous Two-Phase System (ATPS) Volume Ratio:
  • Recovery efficiency ($R_T$) in the top phase: $$R_T = \frac{K \cdot V_R}{1 + K \cdot V_R}$$ where $K = 2.5$ is partition coefficient, $V_R = V_T / V_B$ is the volume ratio of top to bottom phase.
  • Given: Recovery $R_T = 80\% = 0.80$: $$0.80 = \frac{2.5 V_R}{1 + 2.5 V_R}$$ $$0.80(1 + 2.5 V_R) = 2.5 V_R$$ $$0.80 + 2.0 V_R = 2.5 V_R \implies 0.5 V_R = 0.80 \implies V_R = \frac{0.80}{0.50} = 1.6$$
  • Therefore, the phase volume ratio is 1.6:1.
✅ Correct Answer: 1.6:1

question: To have an overall yield of greater than 50% in a three step purification process for a food additive, the minimum average step yield(%) necessary would be around:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Multi-Step Purification Overall Yield:
  • For an $n$-step purification process with an average step yield $y$: $$\text{Overall Yield } Y = y^n$$
  • For a 3-step process ($n = 3$) with $Y > 50\% = 0.50$: $$y^3 > 0.50 \implies y > (0.50)^{1/3} \approx 0.7937 \approx 80\%$$
  • The minimum average step recovery must be 80%.
✅ Correct Answer: 80

question: In a fed batch process for the production of an antibiotic, the dissolved oxygen (DO) level was found to be falling below 30%. If the DO level of 30% is to be maintained in the reactor (without altering the composition of oxygen-air mixture, aeration rate and agitation) then we need to:
options: decrease the volume of the broth by partial withdrawal
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Fed-Batch Feed Rate Control during Oxygen Depletion:
  • When dissolved oxygen (DO) drops dangerously low in fed-batch fermentation:
  • Nutrient excess causes rapid catabolic overflow and high oxygen uptake rate (OUR) exceeding the transfer capacity of the bioreactor.
  • To restore DO levels, the operator must decrease the feed rate of the carbon substrate, slowing microbial growth and reducing oxygen demand.
✅ Correct Answer: decrease the feed rate

question: In a batch sterilization process if ∇overall , ∇heating & ∇cooling are 32.2, 9.8 & 10.1 respectively, THEN the holding time at 121ºC of the process is (given that the specific death rate (k) of microorganisms at 121ºC is 2.54 min-1 ):
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Batch Thermal Sterilization Holding Time:
  • Total sterilization criterion: $$\nabla_{\text{overall}} = \nabla_{\text{heating}} + \nabla_{\text{holding}} + \nabla_{\text{cooling}}$$
  • Calculating the holding period from the Arrhenius rate constant at $121^\circ\text{C}$ gives 4.84 min.
✅ Correct Answer: 4.84 min

question: To achieve complete separation of two pharmaceutical compounds (shown as two peaks in the chromatogram), the relative separation (RS) should be:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chromatographic Peak Resolution ($R_s$):
  • Peak resolution between two chromatographic peaks: $$R_s = \frac{2(t_{R2} - t_{R1})}{W_1 + W_2}$$
  • An $R_s = 1.0$ yields $\approx 98\%$ separation (2% peak overlap).
  • Baseline resolution (complete separation, $>99.7\%$ baseline resolution) required for rigorous pharmaceutical quantification requires $R_s \ge 1.5$.
✅ Correct Answer: ≥ 1.5

question: The anticancer drug, Halichondrin – D is isolated from:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Marine Natural Products (Halichondrin B/D):
  • Halichondrins (such as Halichondrin B and D) are potent polyether macrolides that bind to tubulin and inhibit microtubule dynamics.
  • They were originally isolated from the marine sponge Halichondria okadai (and led to the synthetic anticancer drug Eribulin).
✅ Correct Answer: Sponges

question: Heparin is a:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemical Nature of Heparin:
  • Heparin is a highly acidic sulfated glycosaminoglycan (sulfated polysaccharide) consisting of repeating disaccharide units of sulfated D-glucosamine and D-glucuronic/L-iduronic acid, which acts as an anticoagulant by activating Antithrombin III.
✅ Correct Answer: Sulphated polysaccharide

question: The only naturally transformable marine cyanobacteria is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Natural Genetic Competence in Marine Cyanobacteria:
  • Agmenellum quadruplicatum (Synechococcus sp. strain PCC 7002) is a unicellular marine cyanobacterium that possesses natural genetic competence for transformation with exogenous DNA.
✅ Correct Answer: Agmenellum sp.

question: Marine chemosynthesis is mainly based on:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemosynthetic Carbon Fixation in Marine Ecosystems:
  • At deep-sea hydrothermal vents and cold seeps, primary production does not rely on sunlight.
  • Chemolithoautotrophic bacteria oxidize inorganic chemical donors ($ ext{H}_2 ext{S}, ext{CH}_4, ext{H}_2$) to fix carbon dioxide ($ ext{CO}_2$) into organic biomass via the Calvin-Benson or reverse TCA cycle.
✅ Correct Answer: Carbon dioxide

question: Which one is a DNA replication blocking agent produced by sponges?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Spongonucleosides from Marine Sponges:
  • Arabinosyl nucleosides (spongothymidine and spongouridine, spongosides) isolated from the Caribbean marine sponge Cryptotethya crypta act as competitive inhibitors of DNA polymerase and viral reverse transcriptase, serving as the structural prototypes for antiviral (Vidarabine/Ara-A) and anticancer (Cytarabine/Ara-C) pharmaceuticals.
✅ Correct Answer: Spongosides

question: Eutrophication in aquatic ecosystems is due to reduction of:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Eutrophication & Hypoxia in Aquatic Ecosystems:
  • Eutrophication triggers dense algal blooms. When these blooms collapse, aerobic decomposers multiply exponentially and consume virtually all dissolved oxygen, producing lethal hypoxia.
✅ Correct Answer: Oxygen

question: Halotolerant and halophilic microbes can be isolated from ------ and -------, respectively. P. Sea Q. River R. Lake S. Estuary
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Halophilic Microorganisms Sources:
  • Halophiles require elevated salt concentrations ($ ext{NaCl} > 1.5 - 3\text{ M}$) and are isolated from hypersaline environments such as salt pans and solar salterns (S and P).
✅ Correct Answer: S and P

question: Heavy metal pollutants like Cd and Hg inactivate enzymes by interacting with:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Heavy Metal Poisoning and Thiol Group Reactivity:
  • Toxic soft heavy metals such as Cadmium ($ ext{Cd}^{2+}$) and Mercury ($ ext{Hg}^{2+}$) have extremely high chemical affinity for sulfhydryl (thiol, $-SH$) groups.
  • They inactivate vital cellular enzymes by covalently reacting with the catalytic cysteine residues, forming mercaptides and disrupting disulfide crosslinks.
✅ Correct Answer: cysteine

question: Which of the following class of enzymes initiates aerobic degradation of aromatic pollutants (like naphthalene) in bacteria?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Aerobic Biodegradation of Hydrocarbons:
  • The initial activation and oxygenation of recalcitrant aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons during aerobic biodegradation is catalyzed by oxidoreductases:
    • Monooxygenases: Incorporate one atom of oxygen into the substrate (forming alcohols).
    • Dioxygenases: Incorporate both oxygen atoms of $ ext{O}_2$ to cleave aromatic rings into catechols.
✅ Correct Answer: Oxido-reductases

question: Which one of the following organisms is NOT able to perform light harvesting reaction?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Non-Phototrophic Diazotrophs:
  • Rhodospirillum, Rhodobacter, and Chlorobium are phototrophic bacteria that fix nitrogen using light energy.
  • Azospirillum is a heterotrophic, microaerophilic rhizobacterium that fixes nitrogen using chemical organic carbon sources, and is not able to perform light-driven energy conversion.
✅ Correct Answer: Azospirillum

question: In the soil environment, which one of the following factors is responsible for the biotic stress on the microbial community?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Biological Factors in Soil Genesis:
  • Soil structure and organic breakdown are maintained predominantly by the diverse soil microflora (bacteria, actinomycetes, mycorrhizal fungi).
✅ Correct Answer: Microflora

question: Match the enzymes in Group I with their appropriate role in the environment from Group II: Group I: 1. Laccase 2. Catalase 3. Nitrogenase 4. Cytochrome p450 Group II: P. Xenobiotic detoxification Q. Nitrogen fixation R. Lignin degradation S. Neutralization of toxic O2 species
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Enzymes in Environmental Biotechnology:
  • 1. Laccase: Copper-containing polyphenol oxidase that cleaves recalcitrant aromatic polymers in lignin degradation (1-R).
  • 2. Catalase: Decomposes hydrogen peroxide ($2 ext{H}_2 ext{O}_2 ightarrow 2 ext{H}_2 ext{O} + ext{O}_2$) for neutralization of toxic $ ext{O}_2$ species (2-S).
  • 3. Nitrogenase: Multi-subunit Mo-Fe enzyme that reduces atmospheric $ ext{N}_2$ to ammonia during biological nitrogen fixation (3-Q).
  • 4. Cytochrome P450: Heme monooxygenase involved in phase I xenobiotic detoxification (4-P).
✅ Correct Answer: 1-R; 2-S; 3-Q; 4-P

question: Which one of the following types of mutation would usually NOT be detected in a molecular diagnostic test that is based on sequencing each exon of a gene individually from a male suspected of having an X-linked disorder?
options: Inversion of a part of the gene
correct_answer: Inversion of a part of the gene
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Limitations of PCR Screening in Gene Mutations:
  • Standard diagnostic PCR across flanking primers easily detects:
    • Deletions (PCR product is smaller or absent).
    • Duplications / Insertions (PCR product is larger).
  • However, an internal inversion of a part of the gene retains identical length, primer-binding sites, and overall amplicon size, and thus would usually NOT be detected by simple size-fractionated agarose gel electrophoresis of PCR products.
✅ Correct Answer: Inversion of a part of the gene

question: A couple came for counselling following three first-trimester miscarriages and underwent chromosomal analysis. The man was found to have pericentric inversion with the karyotype 46,XY,inv8(p12q22). Which one of the following would be a correct conclusion?
options: This is a normal variant, likely of no significance
This is an abnormal chromosome that would cause congenital anomalies if transmitted to a child.
This rearrangement might lead to chromosomal imbalance in an offspring and could explain multiple miscarriages.
This rearrangement might cause dicentric or acentric chromosomes in an offspring, which would probably not be compatible with survival.
correct_answer: This rearrangement might lead to chromosomal imbalance in an offspring and could explain multiple miscarriages.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Reciprocal Chromosomal Translocations & Recurrent Pregnancy Loss:
  • Balanced reciprocal translocations in phenotypically normal carrier parents lead to quadrivalent pairing during Meiosis I.
  • Alternate segregation produces balanced gametes, but adjacent-1 and adjacent-2 segregations generate unbalanced gametes with large segmental duplications and deficiencies, causing early embryonic lethality and multiple first-trimester miscarriages.
✅ Correct Answer: This rearrangement might lead to chromosomal imbalance in an offspring and could explain multiple miscarriages.

question: Unequal crossing over between two Alu repeats can lead to an LDL receptor gene with an internal deletion or duplication. Based on this information, which of the following must be true?
options: The LDL receptor gene contains one and only one Alu repeat sequence.
The LDL receptor gene does not contain Alu repeat sequences.
The genome contains only one copy of the Alu repeat sequence.
The LDL receptor gene contains at least two Alu repeat sequences
correct_answer: The LDL receptor gene contains at least two Alu repeat sequences
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Alu-Mediated Non-Allelic Homologous Recombination (NAHR):
  • Unequal crossing over between homologous repetitive elements requires the physical presence of multiple repetitive sequences on the same chromosome.
  • Recombination between two distinct Alu repeats in the LDL receptor gene (causing familial hypercholesterolemia deletions) is possible only because the LDLR gene contains at least two Alu repeat sequences that can mispair during meiosis.
✅ Correct Answer: The LDL receptor gene contains at least two Alu repeat sequences

question: Linkage analysis is performed in a large family with an autosomal dominant hemolytic anemia, using a polymorphic marker within the β-globin locus. The LOD score at q=0 is negative infinity. The LOD score at q=0.01 is -4.5. You conclude that the disorder in this family is:
options: not due to a -globin gene mutation
an acquired disorder, due to a somatic gene mutation
due to a mutation in a gene on chromosome 11, 10 cM centromeric of -globin
correct_answer: not due to a -globin gene mutation
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Linkage Exclusion in Genetic Mapping:
  • In parametric linkage analysis, a LOD score ($Z$) below $-2.0$ at a given recombination fraction ($ heta$) is statistically definitive proof of exclusion of linkage.
  • Thus, finding significant negative LOD scores across the $ eta$-globin locus confirms that the family's disease is not due to a $ eta$-globin gene mutation.
✅ Correct Answer: not due to a -globin gene mutation

question: In Li-Fraumeni syndrome most frequent mutation occurs in:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Li-Fraumeni Syndrome and p53 Mutations:
  • Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is an autosomal dominant hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome characterized by early-onset sarcomas, breast carcinomas, brain tumors, leukemia, and adrenocortical carcinomas.
  • Over $75-80\%$ of affected families carry germline loss-of-function mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene (encoding p53) on chromosome 17p13.
✅ Correct Answer: p53

question: Which one of the following promoters is most efficient for transgene expression in mammary gland of livestock?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mammary-Specific Transgene Expression Promoters:
  • In transgenic animal pharming (producing therapeutic recombinant proteins in livestock milk):
  • The bovine or caprine $ eta$-casein promoter directs exceptionally high, tissue-specific expression exclusively in the secretory epithelial cells of the lactating mammary gland.
✅ Correct Answer: Beta-casein

question: Epinephrine is used along with local anaesthetic because of its:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Adrenaline Co-Administration with Local Anesthetics:
  • Epinephrine (adrenaline) is routinely added to local anesthetics (e.g. lidocaine) because of its potent $alpha_1$-adrenergic receptor agonist properties.
  • Stimulation of $alpha_1$ receptors causes local vasoconstriction of cutaneous and mucosal blood vessels, which:
    1. Slows systemic absorption and clearance of the local anesthetic, prolonging its duration of action.
    2. Reduces localized bleeding in the surgical field.
    3. Decreases systemic toxic peak concentrations.
✅ Correct Answer: α-adrenergic receptor agonist properties

question: Founder effects and bottlenecks are:
options: mechanisms that increase genetic variation in a population
two different modes of natural selection
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetic Drift: Founder Effects and Population Bottlenecks:
  • Both the founder effect (a new colony established by a small number of migrants) and population bottlenecks (severe population reduction due to environmental catastrophe) are classic forms of genetic drift.
  • In small populations, random sampling fluctuations dramatically alter allele frequencies independently of natural selection, often resulting in fixation or loss of alleles.
✅ Correct Answer: forms of genetic drift

question: In commercial farms, embryos are routinely recovered by non-surgical methods. On which day are the embryos recovered from the donor cow after the onset of estrus?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bovine Embryo Transfer Timing:
  • In cattle superovulation and embryo transfer (MOET) programs:
  • Embryos travel down the oviduct and enter the uterine horns around Day 5-6.
  • Non-surgical uterine flushing with a Foley catheter is routinely performed on Day 7 post-insemination, when embryos have reached the expanded blastocyst stage and remain enclosed within the protective zona pellucida prior to hatching.
✅ Correct Answer: 7

question: Human mesenchymal stem cells:
options: Can differentiate into only one type of cell
Can differentiate into few types of cells
Can differentiate into all types of cells
correct_answer: Can differentiate into few types of cells
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Differentiation Plasticity of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs):
  • Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are multipotent (not pluripotent) adult stem cells isolated from bone marrow, adipose tissue, or umbilical cord.
  • They have restricted multipotency and can differentiate into a specific subset of mesodermal lineages: osteoblasts (bone), chondrocytes (cartilage), adipocytes (fat), and tenocytes (tendon).
✅ Correct Answer: Can differentiate into few types of cells

question: Vectors are important in transmission of diseases. Match group 1 with group 2. Group 1 Group 2 1 Louse A West Nile Fever 2 Tick B Scrub Typhus 3 Mite C Lyme disease 4 Mosquito D Epidemic Typhus
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Arthropod Disease Vectors and Transmitted Pathogens:
  • Matching vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies, kissing bugs) to their transmitted pathogens (malaria, dengue, leishmaniasis, Chagas) yields 1-D; 2-C; 3-B; 4-A.
✅ Correct Answer: 1-D; 2-C; 3-B; 4-A

question: Which one of the following is an inhibitory neurotransmitter?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] GABA as Major Inhibitory Neurotransmitter:
  • $gamma$-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian central nervous system.
  • Binding of GABA to ionotropic $ ext{GABA}_A$ receptors opens chloride channels, influxing $ ext{Cl}^-$, hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic neuronal membrane, and suppressing action potential generation.
✅ Correct Answer: GABA

question: Huntington‟s disease is clinically characterized by chorea (abnormal involuntary movements). Which part of the brain is responsible for this phenotype?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Neuropathology of Huntington's Disease:
  • Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor dysfunction (chorea), cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbances.
  • Neuropathologically, mutant huntingtin (mHTT) aggregates cause selective, profound atrophy and loss of medium spiny GABAergic neurons in the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) of the Basal Ganglia.
✅ Correct Answer: Basal Ganglia

question: α-Amanitin is a fungal toxin which inhibits eukaryotic RNA polymerases. The three eukaryotic RNA polymerases show differential sensitivity to this toxin. Which one of the following order (higher to lower) is correct with respect to sensitivity towards α-amanitin?
options: RNA POL III > RNA POL II > RNA POL I
RNA POL II > RNA POL III > RNA POL I
RNA POL I > RNA POL III > RNA POL II
RNA POL II > RNA POL I > RNA POL III
correct_answer: RNA POL II > RNA POL III > RNA POL I
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Differential $alpha$-Amanitin Sensitivity of Eukaryotic RNA Polymerases:
  • The fungal bicyclic octapeptide $alpha$-amanitin displays distinct differential inhibition:
    1. RNA Polymerase II: Extremely sensitive; completely inhibited at low concentrations ($10^{-8}\text{ M}$).
    2. RNA Polymerase III: Moderately sensitive; inhibited at high concentrations ($10^{-6}\text{ M}$).
    3. RNA Polymerase I: Insensitive/resistant to $alpha$-amanitin at all physiological concentrations.
  • Sensitivity order: RNA POL II > RNA POL III > RNA POL I.
✅ Correct Answer: RNA POL II > RNA POL III > RNA POL I

question: A primary cell culture can be transformed into a cell line by all EXCEPT:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Viral Oncogenes and Cell Immortalization:
  • Primary human diploid cell cultures undergo replicative senescence after a finite number of population doublings (Hayflick limit).
  • They can be immortalized into continuous cell lines by oncogenic DNA viruses expressing oncoproteins that inactivate p53 and pRb:
    • SV40 large T antigen
    • Human papillomavirus (HPV E6/E7)
    • Adenovirus (E1A/E1B)
    • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV LMP1)
  • Hepatitis B virus (HBV) does not transform or immortalize primary cell cultures in vitro.
✅ Correct Answer: Hepatitis B virus

question: In a randomly breeding population, an autosomal recessive condition affects 1 newborn in 10,000. The expected frequency of carriers will be nearly:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Hardy-Weinberg Carrier Frequency Calculation:
  • Given: Incidence of autosomal recessive disease: $$q^2 = \frac{1}{10,000} \implies q = \sqrt{\frac{1}{10,000}} = \frac{1}{100} = 0.01$$
  • Normal allele frequency: $$p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.01 = 0.99 \approx 1.0$$
  • Frequency of heterozygous carriers ($2pq$): $$2pq = 2 \times 1.0 \times \frac{1}{100} = \frac{2}{100} = \frac{1}{50}$$
  • Therefore, approximately 1 in 50 individuals in the population is a carrier.
✅ Correct Answer: 1 in 50

question: Assessment of the extent of DNA double strand breaks in cultured human cells, following exposure to ionizing radiation, can be done by quantitation of :
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Histone $gamma$-H2AX as a Biomarker for DNA Double-Strand Breaks:
  • When eukaryotic cells are exposed to ionizing radiation, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) activate ATM and ATR kinases.
  • These kinases immediately phosphorylate the variant histone H2AX at Serine 139 in chromatin flanking the break site, forming $gamma$-H2AX foci.
  • Immunofluorescent quantitation of $gamma$-H2AX foci provides the most sensitive, quantitative cytological assay for DNA double-strand breaks.
✅ Correct Answer: phosphorylated histone H2A.X

question: There are reports of more than 100 mutations at different sites of Factor IX that manifests Haemophilia B. This is an example of:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Allelic Heterogeneity vs Locus Heterogeneity:
  • Allelic heterogeneity: The phenomenon where different mutations at different sites within the SAME single gene locus produce identical clinical disease phenotypes (classic examples: $>2000$ mutations in the CFTR gene cause cystic fibrosis; $>100$ mutations in beta-globin cause beta-thalassemia).
  • Locus heterogeneity: Mutations in different gene loci on different chromosomes produce the same clinical disorder (e.g. osteogenesis imperfecta caused by COL1A1 or COL1A2).
✅ Correct Answer: allelic heterogeneity

question: Specificity factor which activates ubiquitin ligase activity of APC/C during separation of sister chromatids is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Anaphase-Promoting Complex (APC/C) Activation:
  • The Anaphase-Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C) is a multi-subunit E3 ubiquitin ligase that triggers the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
  • At metaphase, once all kinetochores are properly attached to spindle microtubules, the regulatory co-factor Cdc20 binds to and activates APC/C ($ ext{APC/C}^{ ext{Cdc20}}$).
  • Active $ ext{APC/C}^{ ext{Cdc20}}$ targets Securin and Cyclin B for proteasomal degradation, releasing active Separase to cleave cohesin complexes and allow sister chromatid separation.
✅ Correct Answer: CDC20

question: In a diploid organism, loss of function mutations produce dominant phenotypes when there is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Haploinsufficiency in Dominant Genetic Diseases:
  • In diploid organisms, each gene has two functional copies.
  • Haploinsufficiency occurs when a single loss-of-function allele produces a dominant phenotype because a 50% reduction in gene dosage/protein product is insufficient to maintain normal wild-type physiological function.
✅ Correct Answer: haploinsufficiency

question: In Mendel‟s dihybrid cross experiment, if the two selected traits were on the same chromosome (linked) and assuming that there is no recombination, what would be the expected genotypic ratio in the F2 generation?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Complete Genetic Linkage in Dihybrid Cross:
  • If two genes are on the same chromosome with zero recombination (complete genetic linkage in coupling, $AB/ab$):
  • The dihybrid $F_1$ individual ($AB/ab$) produces only two types of gametes in equal proportions: $50\%\text{ }AB$ and $50\%\text{ }ab$.
  • Selfing ($AB/ab \times AB/ab$) produces genotypes: $$1\text{ }AB/AB : 2\text{ }AB/ab : 1\text{ }ab/ab$$ which correspond directly to a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio.
✅ Correct Answer: 1:2:1

question: Huntington disease is caused by:
options: Expanded dinucleotide repeats sequence in coding region
Expanded trinucleotide repeats in non-coding region
Expanded trinucleotide sequence in coding sequence
Expanded dinucleotide sequence in non-coding sequence
correct_answer: Expanded trinucleotide sequence in coding sequence
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion in Huntington's Disease:
  • Huntington's disease is caused by an unstable CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion located within the exon 1 coding region of the HTT gene on chromosome 4p16.
  • The expanded CAG tract is translated into an abnormally long polyglutamine (polyQ) tract in the huntingtin protein ($>36-40$ repeats), conferring toxic gain-of-function properties that lead to neuronal death.
✅ Correct Answer: Expanded trinucleotide sequence in coding sequence

question: The following pedigree shows the inheritance of a very rare human disease. What is the most likely mode of inheritance for the disease trait and what is the probability that the second child of III-2 and III-3 will be a son and will also have the disease?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pedigree Analysis of Rare Autosomal Dominant Trait:
  • The vertical transmission pattern across generations affecting both males and females equally indicates autosomal dominant inheritance.
  • For an affected heterozygous individual ($Aa$) mating with a normal individual ($aa$), the probability of passing the disease allele is $0.5$, which combined with conditional pedigree probability yields Autosomal dominant; 0.25.
✅ Correct Answer: Autosomal dominant; 0.25

question: Microscopic evaluation of a post-mortem brain exhibits hyperchromatic areas when stained with glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This suggests activation of:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Reactive Astrogliosis (Gliosis) in Brain Pathology:
  • In neuropathology, injury to the central nervous system (ischemia, trauma, infection) triggers reactive astrogliosis.
  • Astrocytes enlarge, upregulate the intermediate filament GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein), and display hyperchromatic eccentric nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, forming a dense glial scar.
✅ Correct Answer: astrocytes

question: Parasite numbers in the blood of a patient with Trypanosoma brucci (Sleeping sickness) shows the following pattern: Parasites isolated from population 1 and 2 were found to be antigenecially non- cross reactive. The parasite distribution seen may be due to:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Antigenic Variation in African Trypanosomes:
  • In patients infected with Trypanosoma brucei, parasitemia displays cyclical waves of undulating fever peaks and remissions.
  • Each wave is populated by parasites expressing a distinct Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) coat.
  • Through antigenic switching (antigenic variation), rare trypanosomes switch the active VSG gene expressed at the telomeric expression site via homologous gene conversion, evading host neutralizing antibodies.
✅ Correct Answer: Antigenic switching
